1u35tg3:219: The problem with traditional two-stage sensor fusion is that the sources are “different”: LiDAR provides precise geometry, camera provides color, and software algorithms are responsible for aligning the two. Extrinsic calibration drifts over time and vibration, the two perception paths have time lag, and different sensors have different viewpoints and distortion profiles — these three types of error may be tolerable at low speeds, but in high-speed traversal of crowded streets they can directly decide whether an accident occurs. Rev8 bakes Fujifilm’s color science into the L4 chip, outputting color and geometry from the same source, same frame, and same point at the photon level, naturally spatially aligned with no additional software post-processing needed.
1ur8t3b:226: Ouster has long bet on digital architecture, advocating chip iteration over incremental improvements to mechanical and analog solutions. Co-developing L4 with Fujifilm effectively turns a imaging giant’s color-tuning expertise directly into hardware circuits: a detection rate of 20 trillion photons per second means the sensor has headroom for both weak reflections and strong ambient light, while 40 kHz and picosecond-level precision keep point clouds undistorted under high-speed motion. At the application level, this means “one sensor reads traffic signs, judges whether the vehicle ahead is decelerating by brake light color, and generates terrain maps with true color.”
